objects: trans eQTLs; expression networks; marginal SNP-gene tests
assumptions: genome-wide scans across many genes; smaller trans effects
conclusion: Marginal trans-eQTL scans incur a substantial multiple-testing burden and ignore complex expression structure.
span: The detection of trans eQTLs and networks of genes with related expression patterns is hard both computationally and statistically. Testing all genes against all SNPs via tens of thousands of genome-wide scans incurs a substantial penalty for multiple testing. In addition, trans eQTL effect sizes tend to be smaller than cis eQTLs making their detection harder9.

objects: Y[N,L,T]; A[N,C]; B[T,C]; X[C,L]; additive noise
assumptions: pre-processed expression measured across individuals, genes and tissues
conclusion: SDA models an individual-by-gene-by-tissue expression tensor as a sum of products of individual scores, tissue scores and gene loadings, plus noise.
scope: C latent components in a three-dimensional tensor.
span: We use Y to denote the 3D array or tensor containing pre-processed gene expression measurements. Y has dimensions N × L × T where N is the number of individuals, L is the number of genes and T is the number of tissues. We model Y as follows Y_{n l t} = ∑ c = 1 cA_{n c} B_{t c} X_{c l} + ε_{n l t}

objects: individual score vectors; tissue score vectors; identity covariance matrices
conclusion: Independent standard multivariate normal priors on the individual and tissue scores encode prior independence of individuals and tissues.
scope: Basic prior; separate related-individual extension is outside this method card.
span: We put a standard multivariate normal prior on the component vectors in both scores matrices. P (a·c ) = NN (a·c |0, IN ), P (b·c ) = NT (b·c |0, IT ). (8) This corresponds to a prior belief that individuals and tissues are independent.

assumptions: variational approximation to the SDA posterior
conclusion: Following Titsias and Lazaro-Gredilla, SDA retains dependence between slab weights and inclusion indicators while factorizing the remaining conjugate-parameter factors.
scope: Variational factorization; robustness statement is attributed by the paper to the earlier work.
span: We retain dependence between wcl and scl , rather than assuming they are independent (Titsias and Lázaro-Gredilla, 2011). Titsias and Lázaro-Gredilla (2011) show that this approach results in more robust and accurate estimates. All other parameters with conjugate priors are assumed to fully factorise in the approximate posterior distribution.

objects: psi_cl; phi_cl; rho_c; negative free energy
assumptions: nonconjugate parameters in the variational approximation
conclusion: SDA approximates the nonconjugate sparsity parameters by point masses and optimizes their locations through the negative free energy.
scope: Point estimates within the variational posterior rather than full uncertainty distributions.
span: Unfortunately the parameters ψcl , φcl and ρc do not have conjugate priors and we are not able to use the results from mean field VB. Instead, we specify that their posterior distributions are point masses and optimise the free energy to find these point estimates.

objects: variational posterior mean loadings; PIP = E_Q(S_cl)
conclusion: SDA reports variational posterior mean gene loadings and inclusion probabilities that each loading is nonzero.
scope: PIPs and means approximate the posterior rather than representing exact posterior inference.
span: The form of the VB posterior for every entry of the gene loadings matrix Xcl has the same spike and slab form as the prior. We use this distribution to calculate the expected value, denoted EQ(Xcl). We also calculate a Posterior Inclusion Probability (PIP) that Xcl is not equal to zero, which is equal to EQ(Scl).

objects: observed expression tensor; I_nt observation indicator
assumptions: whole tissue samples missing for some individuals
conclusion: Missing individual-tissue samples are omitted from the likelihood using an observation indicator.
scope: Handles missing tissue samples; no missingness-mechanism guarantee is stated.
span: We deal with missing samples for a given tissue by not including them in the model likelihood. We introduce an indicator variable Int that equals 1 when gene expression has been measured in tissue t for sample n and zero otherwise.

objects: component gene-loading pattern across active tissues
conclusion: A component has a constant gene-loading pattern across the tissues in which it is active.
scope: The authors state that this assumption may fail depending on the dataset.
span: One assumption of our model is that the gene loadings pattern of a component is constant across active tissues, which may or may not be true dependent upon the dataset being analyzed.

assumptions: the specified SDA variational algorithm and its parameter updates
conclusion: Each parameter update is guaranteed to increase or leave unchanged the negative free energy.
scope: Monotone variational objective updates; no global optimum is guaranteed.
span: Our VB algorithm consists of iteratively updating each parameter given current estimates of the other parameters. All updates are guaranteed to increase (or at least not decrease) the negative free energy.

assumptions: complex high-dimensional model fitted using VB
conclusion: The VB algorithm has no guarantee of reaching a global optimum of the marginal-likelihood bound.
scope: Repeated runs can recover different components.
span: The model is complex and has a large number of parameters and there is no guarantee that the VB algorithm will find a global solution when optimizing the bound on the marginal likelihood.

assumptions: latent tensor factors; especially dense components active in one tissue
conclusion: Components are not fully identifiable: paired sign flips leave the fit unchanged, scaling is only partly constrained, and dense factors can retain rotational invariance.
scope: Sparsity partly addresses rotational invariance but does not establish full identifiability.
span: The sign of the gene loadings, individual scores and tissue scores is not fully determined by the model, so that swapping the sign of any two of these parts of the model will produce an equivalent model 56 fit. Scaling of the components is constrained to some extent by the fixed unit variances used in the priors on the individual and tissue scores. The use of sparsity in the gene loadings goes some way to ensure that components are not rotationally invariant, but dense factors will clearly suffer from this problem, especially if they are active in only one tissue.

conclusion: The underlying tensor decomposition is the PARAFAC, also called CANDECOMP, model.
scope: Relationship of the tensor structure; Bayesian sparsity priors are additional modeling choices.
span: This model is known in the literature as the PARAFAC (parallel factors) decomposition or CANDECOMP (canonical decomposition) (Carroll and Chang, 1970; Harshman and Lundy, 1994).
